newsitem.title: USA: IRS removes forward-contracting tax threat for now.
newsitem.headline: IRS removes forward-contracting tax threat for now.

text.p: U.S. Internal Revenue Service, responding to an uproar in farm country, said Tuesday that farmers could file U.S. income taxes as usual and without threat of huge tax bills from use of so-called forward contracts to sell grain.

"This is good news for farmers who want to comply with the tax law and properly report this income on their returns," said IRS Commissioner Margaret Richardson. "They should complete their 1996 returns as they have been doing in the past or as they have been directed to after an IRS audit."
Bills were pending in the House and Senate to make it clear that forward contracts, a popular merchandising tool for farmers, were excluded when the alternative minimum tax is calculated.
They were excluded in the past but Congress dropped the wording in the 1986 tax reform law -- an oversight, according to farm-state lawmakers who accused the IRS of over-reaching.
"Farmers should not be taxed on income they have not received. That defies all common sense," Senator Byron Dorgan, North Dakota Democrat, said in applauding the IRS announcement.

Concern was sparked by an IRS decision last year, in a dispute involving a potato farmer, to require the farmer to count all income from a forward contract in the year the contract was signed although part of the money would not be received until the next calendar year.
Forward contracts are used by farmers to "lock in" favorable prices or to balance income against expenses. Contracts commonly call for delivery and payment months in the future.
Lawmakers said IRS had tried to apply its interpretation in other cases. Under that scheme, one said, a farmer in his area faced $30,000 in axes, nearly equal to the man's income.
Groups such as National Grain and Feed Association have said forward contracts remained a legitimate marketing tool.
IRS also said it would make it easy for farmers to change accounting methods, if they wished, for 1997 and later income.

"Farmers who change their method of accounting in accordance with this procedure will then receive audit protection with respect to the use of an impermissible method of accounting for all taxable years prior to the change," IRS said.
It would waive the user fee, typically $500-$900, to make the change. Farmers should attach Form 3115 to their 1997 income tax returns, which would be due in early 1998.
